title: Job Redesign, Work Rotation, and Early Escalation

content.overview: The strongest safety improvement often comes from changing the work system rather than repeatedly reminding individuals to be careful. Ladder tasks can be eliminated by relocating service points; forceful tool tasks can improve with better tools or fixtures; manual handling can improve through container size, carts, lift assists, storage height, or layout; repetitive work can be redesigned around meaningful task variation. This final lesson turns hazard recognition into a practical improvement cycle.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberate change to equipment, layout, sequence, load, work height, staffing, or method intended to reduce exposure while preserving the task outcome.
Planned movement between tasks with meaningfully different exposure patterns rather than simply changing locations while repeating the same physical demand.
Reporting a developing equipment, workload, discomfort, access, or design problem before it becomes an injury, equipment failure, or production incident.

sections.title: Prioritize system changes
sections.body: Start with the condition creating exposure. Can a frequently serviced sensor be lowered? Can heavy material be stored between knee and shoulder height? Can a smaller container reduce load? Can a cart, fixture, or tool change eliminate sustained grip force? Can a hose route reduce pulling? Can a stable platform replace repeated ladder repositioning? System changes should be considered before relying only on memory, motivation, stretching, or personal strength.

sections.title: Make rotation reduce exposure
sections.body: Rotation is useful only when the next task changes the stressed body regions, force, posture, or repetition enough to provide recovery. Moving a worker from repetitive trimming to repetitive hand pruning may not meaningfully reduce hand exposure. A better rotation plan examines the actual demands of each task, workload peaks, staffing, and recovery time. Rotation should complement—not replace—equipment and layout improvements when those are feasible.

sections.title: Use a closed-loop improvement record
sections.body: When workers report a recurring access problem, damaged tool pattern, difficult lift, or ergonomic concern, capture enough information to act: task, location, equipment, frequency, observed exposure, immediate control, owner, due date, and outcome. After the change, verify whether the original exposure was actually reduced and whether a new hazard was created. A lightweight record turns safety feedback into operations improvement instead of an informal complaint that disappears at shift change.

workedExamples: Workers repeatedly climb to reset an accessible environmental device. Relocating the interface to a serviceable height can remove hundreds of future ladder exposures instead of writing another reminder about ladder use.

A team rotates between trimming and defoliation but both tasks require similar repetitive hand force. Replacing part of the rotation with record review, scouting, or another task with a different exposure profile may provide more meaningful recovery.
commonMistakes: Calling a reminder, poster, or stretching program 'ergonomic redesign' while the physical task remains unchanged.
Rotating workers between tasks that have nearly identical force and repetition demands.
Closing a safety action when the change is installed without verifying whether exposure actually improved.
content.practicalApplication: Complete a mini redesign exercise for one cultivation task. Document the original exposure, propose one engineering/layout/equipment change, one administrative or workflow change, and one escalation trigger. Define how the team would verify the change after implementation.
content.summary: Safety improves fastest when recurring exposures become redesign opportunities. Change the equipment, layout, load, access, or workflow where practical; use rotation only when it meaningfully changes exposure; and close the loop by verifying results.
